passages.t: ‘Do you judge uprightly?’: rulers who serve injustice
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “For the choirmaster. To the tune of ‘Do Not Destroy.’ A Miktam of David” (verse 1). Then the psalm turns on the people in power and puts them on trial. “Do you indeed speak justly, O rulers? Do you judge uprightly, O sons of men?” (verse 1).

The answer is no. “No, in your hearts you devise injustice; with your hands you mete out violence on the earth” (verse 2). Their lying goes back as far as they do. “The wicked are estranged from the womb; the liars go astray from birth” (verse 3).

They will not listen to any warning. “Their venom is like the venom of a snake, like a cobra that shuts its ears, refusing to hear the tune of the charmer” (verses 4 and 5).
passages.hearers:
Israel's law was strict about judges. “Do not deny justice or show partiality. Do not accept a bribe” (Deuteronomy 16:19). A corrupt court was not only unfair. It broke the covenant with God. The prophets often attacked judges who took bribes and crushed the poor.

The first word for ‘rulers’ is hard. The Hebrew as written reads ‘silence’, which makes little sense. Many translators change one vowel and read ‘mighty ones’ or ‘gods’. The BSB puts ‘rulers’. Some think the psalm speaks to human judges, who held God's authority to judge. Psalm 82 has a similar scene. Others think it speaks to unseen powers behind unjust rulers. Either way, the people who should protect the weak are harming them.

Snake charmers were known across the ancient world. The charmer played a tune to control the snake. This cobra ‘shuts its ears’. Nothing can reach it.
passages.later:
Amos cried out for the same thing as this psalm: “But let justice roll on like a river, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream” (Amos 5:24).

Jesus told of a widow who kept going to an unjust judge until he gave her justice. He asked, “Will not God bring about justice for His elect who cry out to Him day and night?” (Luke 18:7).
passages.asks:
This psalm begins where many people are: watching powerful people get away with harm. It does not pretend that is fine. It names it.

Ask who the ‘rulers’ are in your world: in a school, a workplace, a town, a church. Where power is used against the weak, God sees it. And if you have any power over others, the psalm's first question is for you too: do you judge uprightly?

passages.t: ‘O God, shatter their teeth’: a cursing psalm at full force
passages.happening:
Now the prayer becomes fierce. “O God, shatter their teeth in their mouths; O LORD, tear out the fangs of the lions” (verse 6). It asks that the wicked vanish like water running off into the ground, and that their arrows be blunted (verse 7). It reaches for pictures of things that come to nothing: “Like a slug that dissolves in its slime, like a woman’s stillborn child, may they never see the sun” (verse 8). They will be swept away before a cooking pot can feel the fire (verse 9).

Then come the hardest words. “The righteous will rejoice when they see they are avenged; they will wash their feet in the blood of the wicked” (verse 10).

The psalm ends with what people will say. “There is surely a reward for the righteous! There is surely a God who judges the earth!” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
The prayer is aimed at rulers who use violence against the helpless. It is spoken from the side of their victims. To the first hearers, ‘teeth’ and ‘fangs’ were the power to hurt. To break them was to make the attacker harmless.

The pictures of verses 7 and 8 all say one thing: let their power drain away to nothing. Verse 9 is among the hardest lines in the Psalms to translate. It seems to picture a quick fire of thorns under a pot, and a storm that sweeps everything away before the pot is even warm.

Washing feet in blood is a picture from the battlefield. It means a victory so complete that the oppressors are gone.

Notice what the people say at the end. They do not praise the psalmist. They say, ‘There is a God who judges.’ The prayer is for God's justice to be seen.
passages.later:
The cry for justice runs to the end of the Bible. The martyrs in heaven ask, “How long, O Lord, holy and true, until You avenge our blood” (Revelation 6:10). Later heaven sings that God “has avenged the blood of His servants” (Revelation 19:2).

Yet Jesus said, “love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44). And Paul wrote, “Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God’s wrath” (Romans 12:19). A Christian reads Psalm 58 with both of those in hand.
passages.hard:
This is one of the hardest passages in the Psalms, and the book page lists verse 10 among them. These notes do not soften the words. They say what they say.

The book page's part on the cursing psalms sets out four ways Christians read lines like these: as honest prayer that hands vengeance to God instead of taking it; as the voice of people crushed by injustice; as prayers changed by the cross, where Jesus prayed for those who killed him; and as words Scripture records honestly but that are not for Christian lips. Thoughtful believers hold each view, and these notes do not choose between them. One thing is not open: no reading of this psalm has ever made it right to harm anyone.

If you have lost a baby, verse 8 may be painful to read. The psalm uses the picture only to mean something that comes to nothing. It says nothing about your child, whom God knows, or about you.
passages.asks:
Psalm 58 is not a pattern for how to feel about people you dislike. It is a cry from people who have been crushed by those meant to protect them.

If you have been wronged like that, the psalm lets you bring your anger to God in words as strong as you need. Then it leaves the judging to him. If you have not been wronged like that, read it slowly, and let it teach you how much injustice hurts.
